summary: AstroGuardian is a visual health self-assessment tool for astronauts on long-duration missions, where help from Earth is delayed. Each crew member has a profile with an anatomical body figure. Clicking the brain, lungs, heart, gut, bones or whole body opens a page showing related indicators: heart rate, blood pressure, blood oxygen, blood sugar, temperature, sleep, mood and exercise. Astronauts enter their own readings and see trend charts and color-coded status (Nominal, Watch, Alert) at a glance. Each page explains how spaceflight conditions such as isolation, low gravity and closed cabins affect that body system, how to take the measurement, and what to do, including when to contact the flight surgeon. It runs entirely in the browser using simulated data for a fictional six-person crew.
details:
AstroGuardian is a visual health self-assessment tool for astronauts on long missions, where help from Earth is delayed. It shows a six-person crew. Each person has a profile with a clickable anatomical body figure. Clicking the brain, lungs, heart, gut, bones and muscles, or whole body opens a page for that body system. It covers eight indicators: heart rate, blood pressure, blood oxygen, blood sugar, body temperature, sleep, mood and exercise.

Each page shows a trend chart against the normal range, a color-coded status (Nominal, Watch or Alert), how to take the measurement, how spaceflight hazards such as radiation, isolation, low gravity and closed cabins affect that body system, and what to do, including when to contact the flight surgeon. Astronauts can enter new readings and see the charts and colors update. A crew overview shows who needs attention at a glance.

Benefits and impact: it helps astronauts spot problems early and understand what a reading means without assuming medical knowledge. It supports decisions and does not diagnose.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, SVG for the body figure and charts, a WebGL shader for the opening water effect (adapted from the WaterRippleImage component on 21st.dev), Playwright for testing, GitHub for the code, and Vercel for hosting. AI tools, including Claude, helped write the code, and the six crew portraits are AI-generated images of fictional people.

Creativity: a dark water opening screen and hand-drawn logo, a clean clinical body figure that works as a map of health, and plain-language guidance on every page.

Factors considered: communication delay, astronauts needing to assess themselves, simple explanations, and privacy. The tool runs entirely in the browser with no server, so readings stay on the device. The crew and health data are simulated and the normal ranges are general reference values, so it is a prototype for demonstration.
dataRefs: NASA Human Research Program: Five Hazards of Human Spaceflight
